The world has never been more complex, and yet, at the same time, it feels like we've been rewinding, circling back to questions as old as human speech itself. The rituals might have changed, the technologies have, but there are fundamental questions—about identity, belonging, purpose—that echo through the ages. I could talk about the formidable march of artificial intelligence and the ways its shadow already mingles with every facet of human existence. I could dig into climate anxiety, the nebulous psychology of living through multiple crises. Or I could choose to stay at the level of the personal: the way mornings feel on a rainy day, the visceral comfort of a well-worn book, the strange warmth of strangers’ kindness in moments when you needed it most.

It’s tempting to cover all of it at once. Maybe I should. But there is something to be said about locking onto one idea, letting it expand like a ripple across a lake, before you take the next step.

So let’s talk about stories.

Stories are old as firelight. When we share them, we are doing what the earliest humans did while huddled against night and cold. But here's something: today, our stories are not just told around a campfire. They appear in the quiet scroll of our screens, they are typed out in millions of messages, they livestream in real time. They shape memes, news, the language we use to describe ourselves. And despite the flood of new mediums, we are still fundamentally scanning for meaning. We have stories on repeat, stories we tell ourselves again and again, stories we hear from others, and the ones we'd rather not say out loud.

What I want to explore is how the stories we choose—or allow—to define us can either trap us or free us. How we navigate the narrative of our lives, and what happens when we have the courage, or the desperation, to rewrite that narrative.

Take, for example, the story about identity. In adolescence we are told to “find ourselves.” We’re handed questionnaires in school to classify our interests, told to pick a major, encouraged to choose a field. Later, in our twenties or thirties, the narrative shifts to “build yourself”—acquire skills, a career, status symbols. Somewhere along the way, we inherit other stories: “I’m the responsible one,” “I’m the fun-loving child,” “I’m the fixer,” “I’m the one who always gets betrayed.” We adopt these not just because they help us operate, but because stories are shortcuts. They are a way for us to navigate an overwhelming world, to predict how we’ll be treated, how others expect us to behave. They give us rules. The problem arises when those stories outlive their usefulness.

Imagine a person who has always identified as “the caretaker.” Their early life was shaped by situations where they had to take responsibility for siblings, cultural expectations, economic necessity. That story—an identity—came in handy; it gave them purpose when they felt powerless. As an adult, they might still carry that story, unconsciously taking on disproportionate emotional labor, feeling guilty when they say “no,” telling themselves they’re selfish if they prioritize their own needs. It becomes a narrative prison, but it’s also familiar. To rewrite it, they need to learn that their worthiness isn’t conditional, that being cared for doesn’t mean they’re unloved or lazy. That process is messy, because it requires confronting deep fear: What if there isn’t a story to fall back on? What if letting go means revealing the parts of them that nobody has loved before—flaws, laziness, silence, grief?

The fascinating part is watching how we do it. Some of us rewrite through trauma. Some through therapy. Some through travel, through art, through relationships that mirror our behavior back to us. Others never quite let go, and the story calcifies like a scar. And yet, even though the story seems immutable, there is always room for revision. Life is the ultimate unpublished novel; the chapters keep appearing, the characters change, and sometimes we get to be the editor.

What about the stories we inherit collectively—the ones about nations, histories, heroes, villains? These tend to be more contentious. They’re tied to politics, to power, to when and how memory is shared. History textbooks are far from neutral. “But the truth is there,” some might say, “we just need to find it.” But every telling is filtered. The victors compile, and the survivors retell. The narrative of a country might exult a glorious past while quietly glossing over the atrocities that made it possible. The stories we allow, the silences we accept—those shape how communities treat each other in the present. When we don’t confront the dark corners, they keep bleeding into the present, like a stain you keep covering with new paint.

I’ve stayed mindful of the stories I tell about myself, but I also watch the stories shared between friends with fascination. Among your closest people, there are stories that get repeated, again and again. “Remember when you failed that presentation?” “You were always the shy one.” “That time we stayed out all night and watched the sunrise.” These stories become anchors. Some keep friendships alive; some trap us in loops of shame or heroism. It’s interesting how a single event can get retold multiple times, the trajectory shifting slightly each time—who is the protagonist, who is the bystander, who is the villain? The storytelling is less about the past than about how we want to be seen now.

Sometimes I wonder about the stories we avoid. In a world that celebrates productivity, what happens to the stories of rest, of boredom? There’s a cultural mythology that says being busy is being important. Zoom calls, inboxes full of unanswered emails, glowing screens at midnight—these are the hallmarks of a productive life in the modern era. But rest, in that narrative, looks suspicious. Yet, what if rest is not absence of story, but part of a different plotline—one of renewal, of listening, of being rather than doing? The stories we tell about productivity influence the rituals we accept. Maybe we need to retell the story so that rest isn’t an indulgence but an act of resistance.

And then there’s joy—the kind that feels ineffable, like a story told in whispers because it’s too fragile to shout. Joy doesn’t often get highlighted in big narratives unless it’s intense—a wedding, a birth, a once-in-a-lifetime event. But what about the quiet joy of folding laundry on a Sunday afternoon, the visceral relief of taking off your shoes after a long walk, the smile that comes without a reason when you catch someone else laughing? Those stories are easily overlooked, but they’re foundational. Maybe the story we need to tell ourselves more often is that our joys matter. They are data points in our emotional map just as much as a crisis.

Maybe I’m romanticizing stories because I’m a product of them. I grew up hungry for them. Books were a portal, movies a language, songs a memory capsule. I remember nights reading under covers with a flashlight, feeling like the characters were breathing beside me. The stories shaped my interior life. They also shaped how I interpreted the world. It’s easy, now, to see where the stories failed me. The hero’s journey was always framed as masculine, the lovers’ tales were almost always heterosexual, the narratives of success were rooted in capitalistic triumphs. When I say “stories,” I include the ones we consume. They infiltrate even when we think we’re immune.

It’s probably good to talk about control, about agency in storytelling. We default to the idea that other forces—institutions, history, expectations—are the authors. But there is a secret, subtle plot twist: the most radical act is sometimes to simply name that you are no longer following the script. The question isn’t always, “What story should I live?” but “Which story am I allowing someone else to tell about me?” Sometimes, it’s a quiet rebellion: “No, I don’t have to be in that role. I can step aside.” What a relief that is. What a terrifying liberation.

And then there’s the fear that rewriting our story will erase the people we once were. But nothing is erased. The story evolves, like a river. The waters carry sediment from upstream, but the landscape changes. Maybe part of our story is not the events themselves but our relationship to them. The same event can be told differently depending on who tells it and who listens. There is also the phenomenon of stories chosen for comfort rather than truth. People cling to narratives because they are safe. The idea of disorder is unbearable. But order isn’t truth. Sometimes, truth is messy, nonsensical, provisional.

Let me tell you a story I learned once, a simple one: A monk once asked a city worker sweeping the streets why he swept the same streets every day. The worker said, “If I don’t sweep, the dust piles up and people slip. It keeps them safe.” The monk nodded and asked, “And what do you tell yourself while you sweep?” The worker said, “I tell myself that I am sweeping the path for thousands who will walk by. It gives me dignity.” It was a small story, but the monk took it with him. Later, when he wandered through the same streets, he saw the worker doing the same job. He looked down and noticed a small, faded sign stuck to the ground that read, “Noticing small moments keeps the world sane.” The monk wrote the story in his journal.

We live in a world too big to fully know. So we tell stories. That’s how we create patterns and meaning. Our stories can be rebellions, comforts, haunts, prayers. The key is to be aware that we are telling them; that we can choose the narrative lens. The lens defines whether we see ourselves as victims or survivors, as protagonists or observers. That matters because math aside, the human experience is mostly narrative. So choose the story that helps you show up, not hide.

Another angle worth exploring is the idea of narrative as it applies to the environment. Many Indigenous cultures tell stories of the land as something alive, revered, and agentic. Modern society largely sees the environment as resource, statistic, commodity. When that happens, we lose voices of stewardship and connection. There’s a story we tell about nature that is patriarchal—dominance, conquest, “man vs. wild”—even though there is nothing more foolish than claiming control over a living planet. Yet our dominant story is one of exploitation. Maybe not in the headlines all the time, but in the everyday actions: disposable plastics, convenience over sustainability, an impulse to name and control. It’s not just policy. It’s story. The story says that nature is something “other,” something we can dominate, so we do. But what if we told a story where the land is kin, and we are learning to work together again? That story would reframe all of our actions. It would make us question consumption, waste, the pace of life.

Of course, stories aren’t just about the big philosophical questions. They show up in tiny spaces. Maybe you are a bartender who hears the same story every night: a friend’s breakup, a customer’s argument, a reflection about their parents. Or perhaps you are a barista counting the minutes between coffee steamers, watching people tuck themselves into corners with laptops and soft music, each carrying a silent narrative. The stories in these spaces—often fragments—are glimpses at the broader human condition. It’s humbling to realize how many stories go unheard, how many moments we miss just because we’re not listening.

I don’t want to forget the heroism in ordinary acts, either. Stories celebrate dinosaurs and rockets, but countless acts of courage happen with no fanfare. A nurse holding a hand in a quiet hospital room. A parent reading aloud to a child while exhausted from work. The person who mends a neighbor’s fence without being asked. Stories like those deserve the spaces of our bookshelves as much as the extraordinary features do. In fact, maybe they should get more attention, because they remind us that living a good story isn’t about accumulation. It’s about presence.

Let me shift, for a moment, to words themselves. Our language is a story. Every word choice carries the weight of tradition, of oppression, of liberation. Consider how we describe discomfort—“I’m fine,” “It could be worse.” Sometimes we hide behind euphemisms, shading truths with palatable stories. But language evolves. When we invent new words, we’re updating the story. Terms like “metaverse,” “climate grief,” “sleep debt”—these appear because the old stories couldn’t speak to the new realities. The same is true for describing ourselves: pronouns, gender identity, mental health. As new narratives emerge, we begin to see ourselves differently.

Part of the therapy process—if you’ve ever done it—is to sit with the stories that make you feel small. You’ll hear questions like, “Where does that belief come from? Is it yours?” The goal is not to discard every narrative. Some provide structure. The goal is to identify which ones support your well-being and which ones perpetuate harm. The tricky part—because I’m writing this here now—is that rewriting takes time, patience, the willingness to fail. There will be setbacks, because stories aren’t updated in one sitting. They require practice, repetition, seeing the new story reflected back in mirrors—the actual people around you who have to witness your change.

And then there is grace. Unless we name it, we forget it. Grace is the story that says, “You are enough as you are, and you can still grow.” It’s not a passive resignation. It’s an active acceptance. If we allow stories of perfection to dominate, we never rest. Grace lets us slip into simpler narratives: “I was kind,” “I showed up,” “I apologized when I was wrong.” These stories don’t need to be loud; they just need to be true.

Maybe what I’m ultimately saying is that a good story has to make room for contradiction. Real life rarely fits a tidy arc. We simultaneously carry regret and gratitude, anger and compassion. The best stories—perhaps the ones that last—are the ones that allow for nuance. They know that people are multi-faceted, sometimes contradictory, often surprising. They’re the narratives that can hold the sadness of endings and the excitement of beginnings.

In the face of all this, what can we do? How do we become better storytellers? I’d say start with listening. Listen to the stories being told to you—really hear them. Let them land in your body before reacting. Then ask: is this story empowering? Is it true? If not, can I retell it in a way that honors the truth but also honors my growth?

Be curious about other people’s stories. Don’t rush to diagnose or fix them. Let them finish. Stories are processes, not conclusions. Some people’s stories aren’t ready to be told, and that’s okay. They might need silence before words. Respect that.

Guard your own story. It’s yours. You don’t need to share every chapter. You don’t need to make it palatable for the world every moment. Sometimes the story is simply a whisper in the dark. That whisper can be enough.

This world is noisy. So the story I’d like to leave you with is simple: be generous with your words, with your presence, with your listening. But also, be strategic. Your story is worth protecting because it’s the thread that weaves your life together. Write it with intention. Edit with courage. Let it be messy, let it be quiet, let it be radiant. Let it be yours.

And in the end, if we take nothing else away, let us remember: stories are not merely entertainment. They are scaffolding. They build the structures we live in, the relationships we nurture, the causes we fight for, the peace we seek. Keep shaping them. Keep rewriting. Keep living them with an open heart and clear eyes.

What could be more radical than that?
